rationale: The Stanford Quicksort benchmark is a tiny, purely compute-bound program whose entire workload is a tight recursive partition/swap loop, so runtime overhead is the binding constraint while size is nearly free. SUB and SPLIT get low RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights and healthy Security/Diversity weights because they are near-free transformations that should apply broadly. FLA is weighted as the primary security lever (flattening the recursive sort/partition control flow destroys the most structural signatures) with a moderate runtime penalty tolerated given the tiny input sizes typical of this benchmark. BCF is kept security-relevant but with a high RuntimeCost weight since its opaque predicates execute inside the hot partition loop. IBR, ICALL, and IGV receive high RuntimeCost weights: indirect branches and indirect calls land directly on the recursive call path and comparison-heavy inner loop, and IGV has little to protect in a program with almost no global state; their CorrectnessRisk weights are also raised because indirect control flow around recursion and stack-frame assumptions is the most fragile interaction in this code shape. The empty static profile (no function features available) means these weights encode conservative prior expectations for a small recursive C benchmark rather than feature-specific tuning.
